references.text: God secures justice for the widow—a fundamental principle in the Mosaic Law regarding the protection of a widow's rights ([ref:5 Mos 10:18|Deuteronomy 10:18]).
A curse on anyone who twists justice against the widow—the Law emphasizes that widows must receive fair treatment ([ref:5 Mos 27:19|Deuteronomy 27:19]).
The prophet Isaiah urges the people to help the widow obtain her rights, reflecting the widow's plea to the judge ([ref:Jes 1:17|Isaiah 1:17]).
Isaiah accuses the leaders of ignoring the widow's case—a parallel to the unjust judge who initially refused to help ([ref:Jes 1:23|Isaiah 1:23]).
God's law forbids oppressing widows and orphans, and God Himself promises to hear their cry—the background for the widow's rightful claim ([ref:2 Mos 22:22-24|Exodus 22:22-24]).
God is the defender of widows—He who judges fairly on behalf of those without protection ([ref:Sal 68:6|Psalms 68:6]).
The prophet Jeremiah urges the practice of justice and righteousness and warns against oppressing the widow, highlighting the widow's claim to fairness ([ref:Jer 22:3|Jeremiah 22:3]).
Jesus draws the conclusion from the parable: God will secure justice for His chosen ones when they cry out to Him—the widow's persistent prayer is answered ([ref:Luk 18:7-8|Luke 18:7-8]).
The devil is referred to as "the adversary" (ἀντίδικος), the same Greek word used for the widow's opponent in the lawsuit ([ref:1 Pet 5:8|1 Peter 5:8]).
The context of the parable: Jesus told it to show that they should always pray and not give up—the widow's perseverance illustrates this point ([ref:Luk 18:1|Luke 18:1]).
